Three pointed stone bridges deep in the pine forest, the surviving works of the kamilostrata or camel road that carried copper, timber and produce from the Troodos mines down to the harbour at Paphos. The route was pushed through the mountains because the coast road was open to corsairs. Kelefos is the largest, a single high hump over the Diarizos; Elia is nearly flat because it spans a deeper gorge; Roudias crosses the Xeros further west. They are traditionally called Venetian, and the traffic they served fits the Venetian century, but no dated inscription survives on any of them and a Lusignan or Ottoman date cannot be ruled out.

en: The largest public work of Ottoman Cyprus, built from 1747 by Ebubekir Pasha, briefly governor of the island, to bring water about ten kilometres from the Tremithos valley at Arpera to the growing port of Larnaca, which until then depended on brackish wells. Water moved entirely by gravity through a buried channel punctuated by some 250 shafts, surfacing in three arcaded spans of which seventy-five arches survive. It supplied the town until 1939 and was repaired in 1854 and again in 1876 at the expense of the pious foundation Ebubekir had endowed. It is the standing argument against the view that the Ottoman centuries built nothing on Cyprus.

en: A hill town on the southern slopes of the Troodos that made its living from needlework and silver rather than from land. Its drawn-thread embroidery, lefkaritika, mixes local white-work with Venetian cut-work patterns, and from the late nineteenth century Lefkara men carried it by ship to Europe and even to Scandinavia and America while the women made it at home. UNESCO added the craft to its intangible heritage list in 2009. In the sixteenth century Lefkara was reckoned among the largest places on the island and it was a fief in the Ottoman period; its population is now under a thousand.

en: The island's copper came back to life here in the twentieth century, on ground already worked in antiquity and buried under ancient slag; the village name means 'Our Lady of the Slag'. The Cyprus Mines Corporation, founded in 1916 by the American Mudd family after Charles Gunther's prospecting from 1914, reopened Skouriotissa and then the far richer Mavrovouni orebody in 1929, built a company town and a pier at Xeros and made copper and pyrite the colony's largest export and largest private employer. Long strikes in 1948 organised by the Pancyprian Federation of Labour marked the birth of modern Cypriot trade unionism. In 1974 the ceasefire line cut the mines from their processing plant and the company left the island; Skouriotissa is again producing copper today.

Hundreds of thousands of tonnes of black smelting slag lie around the mine, the residue of Hellenistic and Roman workings; the modern company found ancient galleries, wooden tools and Roman coins as it cut into the hill. The slag itself was later reprocessed.

The near-abandoned village, with eight residents at the 2001 census, now houses the headquarters of the Argentine-led sector of the United Nations force, a mining settlement turned peacekeeping base.

en: Great banks of black smelting waste, still carrying traces of residual copper, spread across the district and protected as monuments. They are the largest visible remains of the industry that made ancient Cyprus rich.

en: Galleries and shafts driven into the ore body when surface deposits ran out, the earliest underground mining on the island. Roman activity here is well attested but the workings themselves have never been systematically excavated or dated.

en: Roman slag has been found as much as 3 km from the workings that produced the ore, meaning the rock was carried to the fuel rather than fuel to the rock. That is a reversal of Bronze Age practice and a sign of how far the woodland had been cut back.

en: In situ, various sites in the Troodos foothills
The imperial mines and Herod's lease

Under Rome the mines were held directly by the emperor and worked by contract; Josephus records Augustus handing Herod half the revenue and the lease of the rest. Only Amathus, Tamassos and Soli are named as still producing under Rome, a much smaller industry than in the Bronze Age.
